$schema: Original practice tasks written from published curriculum weights + community themes. No exam content.

items.title: Pod stuck in Pending
items.scenario: In namespace `web`, the Pod `checkout-7f9c` has been Pending for ten minutes. Find out why and make it run. Do not change the Pod's resource requests. Write the one-line reason you found to /opt/answers/checkout.txt.
hints: The scheduler tells you the exact predicate that failed.
'Do not change requests' rules out one of the four Pending causes.

solution.cmd: kubectl config use-context k8s-prod && kubectl config current-context
solution.why: Wrong-cluster work scores zero and gives no signal.

solution.cmd: kubectl describe pod checkout-7f9c -n web | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
solution.why: FailedScheduling carries the failed predicate verbatim — 'had untolerated taint', 'Insufficient cpu', or an affinity mismatch.
Confirms which node carries the taint named in the event.
Trailing dash removes the taint; the scheduler retries automatically within seconds.

solution.cmd: mkdir -p /opt/answers && echo 'FailedScheduling: node(s) had untolerated taint {maintenance: true}' > /opt/answers/checkout.txt
solution.why: Tasks that ask for a written answer are graded on the file, so create the directory and cat the file back.

verify: kubectl get pod checkout-7f9c -n web -o wide   # Running
items.gotcha: If removing the taint is not allowed by the scenario, the alternative is a toleration on the Pod — which for a bare Pod means delete and recreate, since tolerations are immutable.

items.title: CrashLoopBackOff with no obvious logs
items.scenario: The Deployment `api` in namespace `payments` is in CrashLoopBackOff. Identify the container exit code and the cause, fix it without changing the image, and save the last 20 log lines from the failing instance to /opt/answers/api.log.
hints: The running container is a fresh restart — its log is empty.
Exit code 137 is not an application error.

solution.cmd: kubectl config use-context k8s-prod && kubectl config current-context
solution.why: Step zero, every task.
Get the actual Pod name; RESTARTS tells you how long this has been going.
--previous reads the instance that died; the live container has no history.

solution.cmd: kubectl describe pod <pod> -n payments | grep -A3 'Last State'
solution.why: Exit code and Reason. 137 + OOMKilled means the memory limit, not the app.
Patches the Pod template and rolls it in one command — no editor, one rollout.

verify: kubectl get pods -n payments   # 1/1 Running, RESTARTS stops climbing
items.gotcha: Exit code 1 means the app itself failed — read the log, don't raise limits. Exit 137 without OOMKilled can also be an external SIGKILL, e.g. a failing liveness probe.

items.title: Node has gone NotReady
items.scenario: `worker-2` shows NotReady. Bring it back. You have SSH to the node. Do not reboot it, and do not drain or delete it.
hints: The Conditions block of describe node carries the kubelet's own message.
A kubelet that never finished starting can only explain itself in the journal.

solution.why: Ready=False carries a message naming the cause — kubelet not posting status, disk pressure, or network not ready.

solution.cmd: ssh worker-2 'systemctl is-active kubelet; sudo journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager -n 50'
solution.why: The journal is the only place a kubelet that crashed on startup reports its config error.

solution.cmd: ssh worker-2 'sudo systemctl restart kubelet && sudo systemctl enable kubelet'
solution.why: If the unit was simply stopped, this is the whole fix; enable makes it survive a reboot.
Covers the other two branches: an empty CNI directory gives 'network plugin is not ready', and a full disk gives DiskPressure.

verify: kubectl get pods -A -o wide | grep worker-2
items.gotcha: If the journal shows a bad flag or a broken config edit, fix /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml — restarting a kubelet with an invalid config just loops it in 'activating'.

items.title: kubectl cannot reach the API server
items.scenario: Every kubectl command fails with 'connection refused' on port 6443. You have SSH to the single control-plane node. Restore the cluster.
hints: You have no kubectl, so no kubectl-based tool is available.
Control-plane components are files on disk.

solution.why: Distinguishes 'the server is down' from 'your kubeconfig points somewhere wrong'.
A missing kube-apiserver.yaml is the fastest possible fix — restore it and the kubelet starts the static Pod within ~20s.
crictl talks to containerd directly, so it works with the API server dead.
The real error: an unknown flag, a bad certificate path, or etcd unreachable.
Back up before editing — a second typo leaves you with no kubectl and no undo. Saving the file makes the kubelet recreate the Pod; there is nothing to restart.

items.gotcha: If the manifest looks correct, check etcd: the API server exits on startup when it cannot reach etcd, and the log says so plainly.

items.title: Service returns nothing
items.scenario: In namespace `shop`, Service `catalog` is reachable but every request times out. The Deployment `catalog` reports 3/3 Pods Running. Fix it.
hints: Running is not the same as Ready.
Check endpoints before you check anything else.

solution.why: An empty ENDPOINTS column proves it is selection or readiness, not routing.
Compare the Pod labels against the Service selector character by character.

solution.cmd: kubectl get pods -n shop   # READY column
solution.why: 0/1 Ready Pods are excluded from endpoints, which presents as a networking fault.

solution.cmd: kubectl describe pod <pod> -n shop | grep -A10 Readiness
solution.why: Port, path or scheme mismatch between the probe and what the app serves.
If the fault is the selector, patching is faster and safer than editing.

verify: kubectl get endpoints catalog -n shop   # non-empty
kubectl run probe --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it --restart=Never -n shop -- wget -qO- --timeout=2 catalog:80
items.gotcha: Also check targetPort against the port the container actually listens on — endpoints can be populated and still refuse connections.

items.title: Back up and restore etcd
items.scenario: Take a snapshot of etcd to /opt/etcd-backup.db. Then restore the cluster from the pre-existing snapshot at /opt/snapshot-prior.db, leaving the original data directory untouched.
hints: The certificate paths are in the etcd manifest — don't recall them, read them.
A restore is three steps and people reliably forget the second half of step two.

solution.why: This cluster's own source of truth for every path you're about to pass to etcdctl.
etcd is mutual-TLS only; all three flags are mandatory or the rejection looks like an outage.
Proves the file is a readable snapshot before you move on.
Restore into a NEW directory — 'leaving the original untouched' is usually part of the task, and overwriting the live dir is unrecoverable.
Change BOTH the --data-dir flag and the etcd-data volume's hostPath.path. The flag is the container's view; the volume maps it to the host.
The kubelet recreates the static Pod on file change — wait for the new container, don't restart anything.

verify: kubectl get pods -A   # the objects from the snapshot are back
items.gotcha: Editing only --data-dir makes etcd read an empty directory; editing only the volume makes it read the old data. Both restores 'succeed'.

items.title: Upgrade a control-plane node
items.scenario: Upgrade the control-plane node `cp-1` from v1.34.x to v1.35.0, including kubelet and kubectl. Leave the worker nodes on their current version. The node must be schedulable when you finish.
hints: The package repository URL is per-minor-version.
kubeadm does not upgrade the kubelet.

solution.why: Evicts workloads and cordons the node before its components restart.
pkgs.k8s.io serves one minor version per repo URL; skip this and every version you ask for is 'not found'.

solution.cmd: sudo apt-mark unhold kubeadm && sudo apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.35.0-1.1 && sudo apt-mark hold kubeadm
solution.why: The packages are pinned; without unhold, apt silently keeps the old version.

solution.cmd: sudo kubeadm upgrade plan && sudo kubeadm upgrade apply v1.35.0
solution.why: 'apply' rewrites the static Pod manifests — this is where the control plane actually changes. Only the first control-plane node uses apply.

solution.cmd: sudo apt-mark unhold kubelet kubectl && sudo apt-get install -y kubelet=1.35.0-1.1 kubectl=1.35.0-1.1 && sudo apt-mark hold kubelet kubectl
solution.why: kubeadm never touches these; they are a separate upgrade.

solution.cmd: sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart kubelet
solution.why: Loads the new unit config and starts the new binary.
The task says schedulable — forgetting uncordon loses the point after all the work.

verify: kubectl get nodes   # cp-1 Ready, VERSION v1.35.0, no SchedulingDisabled
items.gotcha: Only one minor version per upgrade. And every node other than the first control-plane node uses 'kubeadm upgrade node', not 'apply'.

items.title: Scoped RBAC for a ServiceAccount
items.scenario: In namespace `ci`, create ServiceAccount `deployer`. It must be able to get, list, watch, create and update Deployments in `ci` only, and read Pod logs in `ci`. It must NOT be able to delete anything or see anything in other namespaces. Bind it to the existing Deployment `runner` in `ci`.
hints: Two resources, one of them a sub-resource.
Prove it with impersonation, not by reading YAML.

solution.why: The identity the Pod will present.
create role emits the right apiGroups for you (apps for Deployments, "" for Pods). pods/log is a distinct resource — granting pods does not grant logs.
A RoleBinding keeps the grant inside one namespace, which is what 'in ci only' requires.

solution.cmd: kubectl set serviceaccount deploy/runner deployer -n ci
solution.why: Patches the Pod template so the workload actually uses the identity — creating the SA alone changes nothing.

verify: kubectl auth can-i update deployments -n ci --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer   # yes
kubectl auth can-i delete deployments -n ci --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer   # no
kubectl auth can-i list deployments -n default --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer   # no
items.gotcha: If a 'no' comes back as 'yes', look for a second binding — RBAC is additive and system:authenticated grants are easy to miss.

items.title: Install a component with Helm at a pinned version
items.scenario: Install chart `metrics/metrics-server` version 3.12.1 as release `metrics` into a new namespace `observability`, with the value `args={--kubelet-insecure-tls}` set. Then confirm `kubectl top nodes` works.
hints: Learn the key path before you guess it.
A missing --version silently installs the newest chart.

solution.cmd: helm repo add metrics <url> && helm repo update
solution.why: The repo index has to exist locally before search/install can resolve a version.
Confirms 3.12.1 is actually available under that name.
The chart's defaults name every key you're allowed to set. Guessing key paths is the main way Helm tasks are lost.
--create-namespace avoids a separate step; braces are Helm's list syntax for --set.
Confirms the release name, chart version and status in one line.

verify: helm list -A | grep metrics   # STATUS deployed, CHART metrics-server-3.12.1
items.gotcha: If 'kubectl top' still fails, read the metrics-server Pod logs — a TLS error against the kubelet is exactly what that --set flag exists to fix.

items.title: Find and use a custom resource
items.scenario: An operator was installed in namespace `db-operator`. Nothing it should manage is being created. Diagnose the failure and write the offending message to /opt/answers/operator.txt. Also list the custom kinds it registered, with their API group, to /opt/answers/kinds.txt.
hints: There is a fixed order for debugging an operator.
api-resources answers 'what kinds did this add' without a browser.

solution.why: Step 1: are the CRDs registered at all? If not, the bundle didn't fully apply.
Gives the plural name, short name, namespaced flag and kind — everything you need to create an instance.
Step 2: is the controller actually running? CrashLoop or ImagePullBackOff answers the whole task.
Step 3: the controller narrates its own failure — usually an RBAC denial on the resources it watches.
The schema, offline and version-correct, for whatever instance you now have to create.

items.gotcha: 'the server doesn't have a resource type' means the CRD is missing, not that your YAML is wrong. And never delete a CRD to 'reinstall it' — that deletes every instance cluster-wide.

items.title: Default-deny plus one allowed path
items.scenario: In namespace `prod`, deny all ingress and egress traffic by default, then allow Pods labelled `app=web` to reach Pods labelled `app=db` on TCP 5432 only. DNS must keep working for every Pod in the namespace.
hints: Two policies, not one.
A full egress deny breaks DNS unless you allow it back.

solution.why: Faster than the docs tab, and always the right schema version.
An empty podSelector selects every Pod; naming a policyType with no rules denies that direction.

solution.cmd: cat > allow-web-db.yaml   # podSelector app=db, ingress from podSelector app=web, port 5432
solution.why: Policies are additive, so this one re-opens exactly one path through the deny-all.

solution.cmd: cat > allow-dns.yaml   # podSelector: {}, egress to kube-system, ports 53/UDP and 53/TCP
solution.why: A blanket egress deny blocks CoreDNS, and every symptom afterwards looks like a DNS outage.
Apply together so the namespace is never left in the deny-only state longer than necessary.

verify: kubectl run probe --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it --restart=Never -n prod --labels=app=web -- sh -c 'nslookup db; nc -zv db 5432'
kubectl run probe2 --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it --restart=Never -n prod --labels=app=other -- sh -c 'nc -zv -w2 db 5432 || echo BLOCKED'
items.gotcha: Under `from:`, two dashes mean OR and one dash means AND. And if traffic still flows, check whether the CNI implements NetworkPolicy at all — the object applies cleanly either way.

items.title: Expose an app through Ingress
items.scenario: Deployment `storefront` in namespace `shop` listens on container port 8080. Expose it internally on port 80, then route `shop.example.com/` to it through the existing nginx Ingress controller. Requests to /api must go to Service `api` on port 8080 instead.
hints: Both the Service and the Ingress have imperative forms.
Longest-prefix wins; order in the file does not.

solution.why: Copies the Deployment's own labels into the selector — the field most often typo'd by hand.
Confirm the selector matched before layering an Ingress on top of nothing.
The rule syntax is host/path=service:port; a * suffix sets pathType: Prefix. One command, both rules.
Shows the resolved backends and whether the controller has assigned an ADDRESS.

verify: kubectl get ingress -n shop   # ADDRESS populated
kubectl get endpoints storefront api -n shop
items.gotcha: No ADDRESS means no controller is watching, or ingressClassName doesn't match one. A 503 means the backend Service has no endpoints — a different problem entirely.

items.title: Route traffic with the Gateway API
items.scenario: A Gateway named `edge` exists in namespace `infra` with an HTTP listener on port 80. Create an HTTPRoute in namespace `shop` that sends `shop.example.com/checkout` to Service `checkout:8080`. The route is not attaching — find out why and fix it.
hints: Gateway API reports acceptance explicitly, unlike Ingress.
Cross-namespace attachment is not allowed by default.

solution.why: Confirm the Gateway exists and is Programmed before blaming the route.

solution.cmd: kubectl apply -f httproute.yaml   # parentRefs: name edge, namespace infra
solution.why: parentRefs is what binds a route to a Gateway; the namespace field is required for a cross-namespace parent.
status.parents[].conditions names the failure — NotAllowedByListeners or NoMatchingParent.
A listener's allowedRoutes.namespaces defaults to Same, which is exactly why a cross-namespace route silently fails to attach.

verify: kubectl describe httproute checkout -n shop | grep -A5 Conditions   # Accepted True
items.gotcha: If 'kubectl get gateway' says the server has no such resource type, the Gateway API CRDs aren't installed — they don't ship with Kubernetes.

items.title: Roll, break, and roll back
items.scenario: Update Deployment `web` in namespace `shop` to image nginx:1.27, ensuring no capacity is lost during the rollout. The new image fails to start — roll back to the previous revision and record the revision number you returned to in /opt/answers/rollback.txt.
hints: Zero downtime is a two-field answer.
History is numbered; undo without an argument goes back exactly one.

solution.why: maxUnavailable: 0 forces a new Pod Ready before an old one goes — that is what 'no capacity lost' means.

solution.cmd: kubectl set image deploy/web -n shop nginx=nginx:1.27
solution.why: Patches one field, triggers exactly one rollout, no editor.
It will not converge; that is the signal to stop waiting rather than sitting on it for the full progress deadline.
Read the revision numbers before undoing so you can record the right one.

solution.cmd: kubectl rollout undo deploy/web -n shop && kubectl rollout history deploy/web -n shop | tail -3 > /opt/answers/rollback.txt
solution.why: undo without --to-revision goes back exactly one revision.

verify: kubectl rollout status deploy/web -n shop   # successfully rolled out
items.gotcha: A rollout that hangs with new Pods Running but 0/1 is a readiness probe, not the image — and with maxUnavailable: 0 it blocks forever rather than degrading.

items.title: Config, autoscaling and admission
items.scenario: In namespace `dev`: create ConfigMap `app-cfg` from the file /opt/app.env so that each line becomes its own key; inject all of its keys into Deployment `api` as environment variables; then autoscale `api` between 2 and 8 replicas at 70% CPU. Creating the HPA is not enough — make sure it can actually compute a target.
hints: Two --from flags exist and they do different things.
A CPU percentage needs a denominator.

solution.why: --from-env-file gives one key per KEY=value line; --from-file would give a single key holding the whole file.
Writes envFrom correctly in one command — configMapRef with a capital M is a common hand-authoring typo.
--cpu-percent is a percentage OF the request. With no request there is no denominator and the HPA shows <unknown> forever.
One command; no HPA manifest needed.

verify: kubectl get cm app-cfg -n dev -o jsonpath='{.data}'
kubectl get hpa -n dev   # TARGETS shows a number, not <unknown>
items.gotcha: If TARGETS stays <unknown> after adding requests, check that metrics-server is installed — kubectl top will fail the same way.

items.title: Static PV, PVC and a Pod that uses it
items.scenario: Create a 2Gi PersistentVolume named `pv-logs` backed by hostPath /mnt/logs, class `manual`, retained on delete. Create a 1Gi PVC named `pvc-logs` in namespace `ops` that binds to it, and a Pod `logger` mounting it at /var/log/app. The PVC must not use the cluster's default StorageClass.
hints: Nothing here has an imperative generator.
'Must not use the default class' is an instruction about one specific field.

solution.why: PV, PVC and StorageClass are the three kinds with no kubectl generator, so explain is your schema.

solution.cmd: cat > pv.yaml   # capacity 2Gi, accessModes [ReadWriteOnce], persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy Retain, storageClassName manual, hostPath /mnt/logs
solution.why: Retain keeps the data when the claim goes; the class name is what steers the binding.

solution.cmd: cat > pvc.yaml   # requests 1Gi, accessModes [ReadWriteOnce], storageClassName manual
solution.why: 2Gi >= 1Gi, modes match, class matches exactly — those three conditions are the whole binding rule, and naming the class is what avoids the default.

solution.cmd: kubectl apply -f pv.yaml -f pvc.yaml && kubectl get pv,pvc -n ops
solution.why: Confirm Bound before building a Pod on top of an unbound claim.

solution.cmd: kubectl run logger --image=busybox:1.36 --dry-run=client -o yaml -- sleep 3600 > pod.yaml   # add volumes + volumeMounts
solution.why: Generate the skeleton and add only the two stanzas rather than typing a Pod from memory.

verify: kubectl get pvc -n ops   # STATUS Bound, VOLUME pv-logs
kubectl get pv   # RECLAIM POLICY Retain, CLAIM ops/pvc-logs
items.gotcha: storageClassName: "" is not the same as omitting the field. Omitting it silently pulls in the default class, which is exactly what this task forbids.

items.title: PVC stuck Pending
items.scenario: PVC `data` in namespace `analytics` has been Pending for 20 minutes and the Pod that wants it is stuck ContainerCreating. Diagnose and fix it without creating a new StorageClass.
hints: The PVC's events name the cause in plain English.
One of the possible messages is not a fault at all.

solution.cmd: kubectl describe pvc data -n analytics | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
solution.why: Four distinct messages map to four distinct causes; this read decides the branch immediately.
'no-provisioner' means static binding only — no PVC will ever auto-provision against it.
If an Available PV exists, the fault is a mismatch: size, access modes, or class.
A Released PV still points at its old claim; clearing claimRef returns it to Available so it can bind again.

verify: kubectl get pvc data -n analytics   # Bound
items.gotcha: 'waiting for first consumer to be created before binding' is WaitForFirstConsumer working correctly — the fix there is to schedule the consuming Pod, not to touch storage.
